We first applied ordination methods to produce species-specific values on orthogonal trait axes and then used hierarchical clustering to group all butterflies into functional groups based on these species-specific values.
For the ordination, we applied a Hill & Smith principal component analysis (Hill & Smith, 1976) which is appropriate for analyses that contain both categorical and continuous species trait states.

Based on the Cattell’s scree test (Cattell, 1966), we retained the first two ordination axes in the analysis and applied a hierarchical cluster analysis with the unweighted pair-group method using arithmetic averages (UPGMA) to produce a dendrogram of the trait similarities among species.
This was done with the ‘daisy’ function of the R package ‘CALIBRATE’ and the ‘AGNES function of the ‘CLUSTER’ package.

lifeStage.quote: Segregating species into functional groups showed that the highest rate of regional extinction occurred among sedentary habitat specialists overwintering in the egg stage, while the most severe local-scale declines occurred among sedentary host plant specialists

These traits were extracted from the literature on Danish butterflies (Stoltze, 1996; García-Barros, 2000; Frederiksen et al., 2006) and represented overwintering stage, migratory behaviour, degree of habitat openness, habitat specialization, larval host plant distribution, voltinity (number of generations per year), body size and host plant specialization (larval dietary breadth).
cluster 1 (sedentary host plant specialists overwintering in the larval stage)
cluster 2 (sedentary habitat specialists overwintering in the egg stage)
cluster 3 (mobile generalists with mature overwintering stages)

The highest rate of regional extinction occurred among sedentary habitat specialists overwintering in the egg stage (cluster 2), while the most severe local-scale losses occurred among sedentary host plant specialists overwintering in the larval stage (cluster 1).
